c.tagline: Colorful island town on Lake Peten Itza and Guatemala's gateway to the Maya ruins of Tikal.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps in Peten. Short hops around Flores island and Santa Elena are by tuk-tuk (mototaxi) for a few quetzales; longer trips and airport runs are by taxi or hotel shuttle at a fixed price agreed in advance.

emergency.note: 110 reaches the PNC (national police); 122 the volunteer firefighters (bomberos) who also run ambulances; 1500 the municipal firefighters and 1554 the Red Cross. Peten is remote, so hotels and tour operators are often the fastest source of help.

hood_landmark.Cerro / El Remate: El Remate, Lake Peten Itza, Guatemala

avoid.reason: Avoid the back streets of Santa Elena, across the causeway, after dark — petty crime is more common there than on Flores island.
Watch bags at the Santa Elena bus terminal and vet tour/shuttle operators to avoid overcharging scams.

hood_desc: The colorful little island old town on Lake Peten Itza, a grid of pastel houses, cobbled lanes, lakeside restaurants and hostels crowned by the twin-domed cathedral; fully walkable and the atmospheric base most travelers choose for visiting Tikal.

The bustling mainland town across the causeway, home to the airport, bus terminal, banks and markets; less charming but cheaper and convenient, with lakefront hotels and the main transport connections.

The workaday town just west of Santa Elena, the largest and most local of the three, with budget lodging and a couple of lakeshore boutique hotels; quiet and residential, a short tuk-tuk from the island.

A tranquil lakeside village about 30 km northeast toward Tikal, strung along the shore of Lake Peten Itza with swimming spots, jungle lodges and sunset views; a peaceful, nature-focused alternative to the island.

The great Maya city and national park an hour north, where towering limestone temples rise above the rainforest canopy amid howler monkeys and toucans; a cluster of on-site jungle lodges lets you catch sunrise and sunset over the ruins.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water only.

transit.hours: Tuk-tuks run through the day and into the evening; boats and shuttles run on demand or at set departure times arranged the day before.
transit.note: There is no formal public bus network on the island; the flat little town is walkable, tuk-tuks handle Santa Elena and the causeway, lanchas cross the lake to San Andres/San Jose and lakeside lodges, and shuttle vans run the 1-1.5 hr road to Tikal.
transit.pay: Tuk-tuks around Flores island and Santa Elena charge a few quetzales per ride, paid in cash; lake boats (lanchas) and tourist shuttles to Tikal, Yaxha or the border are booked and paid in cash through hotels and agencies.

bus: Terminal Nueva Santa Elena (intercity coaches: Fuente del Norte, ADN, Linea Dorada)
Tourist shuttle vans to Tikal, Yaxha, Belize and Rio Dulce
ferry: Lake Peten Itza passenger lanchas (to San Andres, San Jose, lakeside lodges)

transit.m: Taxi or tuk-tuk to Flores island, ~10-15 min
Hotel shuttle to Santa Elena / Flores when arranged

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants (sometimes already added as 'propina'); small tips for guides, drivers and boatmen are appreciated.

food.name: Pepian
food.desc: Guatemala's national stew - chicken or beef in a dark sauce of toasted pumpkin and sesame seeds, tomato and chillies, served with rice and tortillas.

places.name: Raices Restaurante
places.note: Repeatedly named the island's best traditional kitchen; the pepian is the dish reviewers single out.

places.name: La Danta Restaurante
places.note: Colourful house restaurant cooking with Peten ingredients; well reviewed Guatemalan pepian.

places.name: Restaurante San Telmo
places.note: Straightforward authentic Guatemalan cooking a block back from the water, popular for set lunches.

food.name: Tikin xic
food.desc: Maya-style white fish rubbed with achiote, sour orange and garlic, wrapped in banana leaf and grilled until it flakes - a Peten and Yucatan classic.

places.name: Raices Restaurante
places.note: Grills lake and coastal fish over wood right on the shoreline terrace; sunset tables fill first.

places.name: Restaurante Maracuya
places.note: Lakeside dining room with wide water views and a strong local seafood and fish list.

places.name: Restaurante San Telmo
places.note: Traditional preparations at local prices, including achiote-marinated grilled fish.

food.name: Blanco del lago (fried lake fish)
food.desc: Whole white fish from Lake Peten Itza, fried crisp and served with rice, black beans, fried plantain and a pile of tortillas.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Santa Elena
places.note: Comedor stalls in the mainland market fry lake fish to order for a fraction of island prices.

places.name: Raices Restaurante
places.note: Lakefront grill and fry house that locals rate for whole fish plates.

places.name: Restaurante Maracuya
places.note: Reliable whole-fish plates with the best water views on the island.

food.name: Chirmol with grilled meat
food.desc: Fire-roasted tomato, onion, chilli and coriander salsa spooned over churrasco or grilled chicken - the everyday Guatemalan condiment turned centrepiece.

places.name: La Danta Restaurante
places.note: Peten-sourced grill plates served with house chirmol; lively, well reviewed dining room.

places.name: Restaurante San Telmo
places.note: Churrasco and grilled chicken plates in the traditional style, generous and cheap.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Santa Elena
places.note: Evening grill stands serve meat with chirmol and tortillas to a mostly local crowd.

food.name: Tamalitos and chuchitos
food.desc: Small corn parcels steamed in leaves - plain tamalitos to mop up stew, or chuchitos filled with meat and tomato recado and topped with cheese.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Santa Elena
places.note: Morning tamal vendors sell chuchitos and tamalitos de chipilin fresh from the steamer.

places.name: Raices Restaurante
places.note: Serves tamalitos alongside the stews rather than plain rice, as it is done at home.

places.name: Flores island street vendors
places.note: Baskets of chuchitos appear around the plaza and church in the early evening.

food.name: Kak ik
food.desc: Q'eqchi' Maya turkey soup, brick-red with achiote, coriander seed and chillies, served with rice and tamalitos - one of Guatemala's oldest recipes.

places.name: Raices Restaurante
places.note: One of the few island kitchens cooking the full Maya soup properly to order.

places.name: La Danta Restaurante
places.note: Menu built around Peten and Maya ingredients, with regional soups rotating daily.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Santa Elena
places.note: Market comedores make big pots of turkey and chicken soup for weekend lunches.

food.name: Guatemalan coffee
food.desc: Highland arabica from Huehuetenango and Antigua, poured black or as cafe con leche; Flores cafes roast and brew it properly for the Tikal crowd.

places.name: Cool Beans Cafe
places.note: Long-running garden cafe with lake views, strong coffee and slow breakfasts before the ruins run.

places.name: Maple y Tocino
places.note: Popular brunch spot; espresso drinks alongside the famous four-topping waffle.

places.name: Terrazzo
places.note: Rooftop terrace above the island for coffee and cakes with a sunset view.

food.name: Horchata and agua de jamaica
food.desc: Iced rice-and-cinnamon horchata or tart hibiscus jamaica, ladled from glass jars at every comedor - the standard non-alcoholic pairing with a heavy plate.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Santa Elena
places.note: Jars of horchata, jamaica and tamarindo on every comedor counter, refilled all day.

places.name: Restaurante San Telmo
places.note: House refrescos naturales come with the set lunches; ask for jamaica.

places.name: Raices Restaurante
places.note: Fresh fruit and grain refrescos alongside the traditional food menu.

landmarks: Tikal
The colossal UNESCO-listed Maya city an hour from Flores, where 60-meter temple pyramids pierce the rainforest canopy above howler monkeys.
Lake Petén Itzá
The vast jungle-rimmed lake surrounding Flores island, its glassy waters made for sunset boat rides, swimming and lakeshore villages.
Flores Island Old Town and Malecón
A tiny islet of candy-colored houses, cobbled lanes and a waterfront promenade, all walkable in twenty leisurely minutes.
Catedral Nuestra Señora de los Remedios y San Pablo
The whitewashed twin-towered church crowning the island's highest point, overlooking red rooftops and the lake in every direction.
Yaxhá
A majestic and blissfully uncrowded Maya ruin between two lakes, where sunset from Temple 216 ranks among Guatemala's great travel moments.
Mirador del Rey Canek (Tayasal)
A lakeside viewpoint tower on the peninsula facing Flores, built over remnants of the Itza Maya's final capital, with sweeping island views.
Jorge's Rope Swing
A beloved lakeside hangout across the water from Flores where travelers swing from ropes into Lake Petén Itzá's warm green shallows.
ARCAS Wildlife Rescue Center
A conservation center on the lake's north shore rehabilitating trafficked jaguars, macaws and monkeys, with an educational visitor trail.
Parque Natural Ixpanpajul
A private rainforest reserve of hanging bridges, ziplines and canopy towers just south of the lake, ideal for spotting birds and monkeys.
San Miguel Village and Playita El Chechenal
A mellow lakeside village a short lancha hop from Flores, home to the area's prettiest public swimming beach.

train.note: Guatemala has no passenger railway. The FEGUA network wound down in the 1990s, regular traffic stopped in 1996 and the last heritage steam charters ran in 2007; the Peten never had a line at all. The only rail project in the country is the planned Metro Riel light rail in Guatemala City, still in pre-construction. Everything in and out of Flores therefore moves by road, boat or air.

intl.to: Belize City & San Ignacio (Belize) - via the Melchor de Mencos border, about 2 hrs from Flores
intl.op: Fuente del Norte and Marlin Espadas - tickets at the Santa Elena terminal, some routes online via https://guatego.com/
Linea Dorada / Fuente del Norte - tickets at the Santa Elena terminal

intl.to: Palenque & San Cristobal de las Casas (Mexico) - minibus to Bethel plus a Usumacinta river boat to Frontera Corozal

bus.note: Almost all long-distance buses use the Terminal Nueva de Santa Elena, roughly 2 km from the causeway onto Flores island, with tuk-tuks shuttling across for a few quetzales. Overnight services to Guatemala City take 8-9 hrs and are run by Fuente del Norte, Linea Dorada and ADN, whose first-class buses are worth the extra; most seats are still sold at the terminal counters in cash, though shuttles and some cross-border services can be booked online through GuateGo (https://guatego.com/). For Belize you cross at Melchor de Mencos, which is quick, but note that Belize charges a border fee when you leave it again; for Mexico the paved El Ceibo crossing to Tenosique now has direct minibuses and is faster than the old river route.

intl.to: San Miguel, San Jose & lakeside villages (Guatemala) - lanchas from the Flores waterfront and the Santa Elena embarcadero
intl.op: local lancha cooperatives - pay at the dock

intl.to: Frontera Corozal (Mexico) - Usumacinta river boat from Bethel, about 4 hrs by road west of Flores
intl.op: local boat cooperatives - pay at the landing or as part of a through shuttle ticket

ferry.note: Flores island is joined to Santa Elena by a short causeway, so no boat is needed to reach the town itself. Small lanchas cross Lake Peten Itza on demand from the waterfront to San Miguel, San Jose and the lakeside hotels, charging a few quetzales and running until dusk; there is no fixed timetable and you negotiate at the dock. The only cross-border boat is the Usumacinta crossing from Bethel to Frontera Corozal in Chiapas, a 40-minute river trip usually sold bundled into a Flores-Palenque shuttle package, with Guatemalan exit and Mexican entry stamps done at small posts on each bank.

half.name: Uaxactún
half.blurb: Remote Maya site north of Tikal with an ancient astronomical observatory complex, far quieter than the main ruins.

half.name: Ceibal Archaeological Site
half.blurb: Riverside Maya ruins near Sayaxché, once one of the largest cities in the Petén lowlands, reached partly by boat.
